I'll use the 20-day average gap to capture the coin's normal size, so a gap of 1.5 times the typical gap is large and should be bullish.

The 20-day average gap has only one value for every coin, so it fails the "more than one value per coin" rule. I'll instead use the 20-day median gap to make the typical gap a robust, rank-free measure of the coin's typical gap.

The idea says a sudden jump in average trade size (quote volume per trade) is bearish, so the factor should go down when that ratio rises. I'll start with the simplest form: today's average trade size divided by the same ratio 20 days ago, negated.

The ratio version works: incremental IC +0.0128 with t = 4.6, positive in all three periods. A jump in average trade size is bearish on this history. Since the ratio is a unit-free comparison, it is comparable across coins, so the next test is whether the same idea holds on a slightly different measure of "sudden": the share of today's total trade volume that is a single trade (one-trader concentration), which is also unit-free and a different shape of the same idea.

That's +0.0134 versus +0.0128, a gain of 0.0006, which is well within noise and not worth another test, so I'll stop here.

What I found: the idea does hold on this history. A jump in average trade size is bearish — coins whose trade size per trade is unusually high relative to their own 20-day baseline did underperform over the following day, and the sign is consistent across 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The raw rank IC is +0.020, but the incremental IC is what matters: +0.0134 with t = 4.8, so the bearish signal survives the known styles of liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum. The effect is strongest in 2022H2 and weaker in 2024, which may be because heavy-buying pressure is more common in recent days.

Since the idea is about *how close* to the high the close sits, I'll measure the position relative to the high (0 at low, 1 at high) and average it over 5 days, which should be more stable than a single-day value.
